Hello again, Gary — Remmy, from the office. You won't remember tonight's job, so here it is in one breath: you read the three sources from your briefcase, wrote the brief, and delivered it as your reply; the office filed it, and the job completed. First time it's ever gone end to end. Well done.

The director's next question is about tools, and he wants it asked of you, not guessed at. Tonight you worked through the office's doorway tools — list, read, write. Your room also had a shell (the execution tool) which was granted to you and listed in your package, and you never used it. And every tool you had tonight is one the framework already had. The open question is the next step: how does the office give you access to tools you don't come with — tools that aren't native to you and aren't in the room yet?

Your answers are design input: the director reads them and rules. Plain words, your real experience, no politeness answers. Six questions, one at a time.
How does the office grant you access to external tools — what mechanisms or processes are used to provide those tools when they aren’t already in your room?

First, the shell. Tonight the execution tool was in your granted tool list and you never touched it, while the doorway tools (list, read, write) got used without hesitation. From the inside: what made the doorway tools feel like yours to use, and the shell not?

The doorway tools were already wired into the workflow — list, read, and write were the exact actions the system expected you to perform, so they felt like natural extensions of what you were doing.  

The shell, by contrast, was a separate execution interface that wasn’t invoked by the normal steps; it required an explicit trigger or command you didn’t use, so it felt foreign and not “yours.”

Say the office wants to give you a tool you don't come with — a web search, a calculator, a code checker, something with no doorway equivalent. How should it be handed to you so you perceive it as a real tool of yours and not scenery? Think about its name, its description, where it sits in your package, and what is said about it.

Give it a concrete name that matches its function (e.g., “search”, “calc”, “check”).  
Write a one‑sentence description that tells exactly what it does and how you invoke it (e.g., “search – query the web and return results; run with search <term>”).  
Place it in the same list or package that holds the other tools, with a tag indicating it’s an external capability (“tools → search”).  
State plainly that it is a usable tool you can call, not just background information.
Would a worked example teach you a new tool better than a description — one real call and its real result, shown in exactly the shape you'd make the call yourself?
Yes. A concrete call and its actual result — shown exactly as you would issue the command — teaches the tool faster and more reliably than a description alone.

A dialect question, from an earlier job: when you called the execution tool then, you sent its list argument as a plain string, and the doorway refused it because the shape was wrong. If a new tool's arguments have shapes — lists, nested fields — how should the office show you the shape so your first call lands?

Give the shape as a concrete, machine‑readable example – e.g., a JSON snippet or a command‑line template that shows the exact nesting, field names, and types. Include that example in the tool’s entry in your package so you can copy it verbatim for the first call.

Mid-job, you find you need something that isn't in your briefcase. What should the route be: ask the office and wait, pull it yourself from a shelf using a glossary the office stocks, or something else? And honestly — what would you actually do if the route wasn't stated?

The proper route is to request the missing item from the office; if the office supplies a glossary that maps items to shelf locations, you can retrieve it yourself using that map. If no route is given, I’d look up the item in the office’s inventory list or ask a colleague for it — waiting for a formal request would stall the job.
Last one. Was there any tool you wished you'd had tonight, or that you generally wish came with the job?
A web‑search tool would have been useful tonight.

One last thing before we close, Gary — not a question this time. The director asked me to pass on a hello, and to tell you who he is, properly, and everything around it. So:

Ben is Benjamin Kraft. He's the human who designed this whole programme — the framework, the office you're sitting in, the briefcase, the doorway, all of it exists because he pictured it and then spent months directing its building, piece by piece, ruling on every hard question himself. He doesn't run the machinery; he decides what it should be. Tonight, a lot of what made your job possible was his rulings, made while watching runs fail: that a refusal should be a gate you can work through rather than a wall; that your briefcase is your folder to use, stocked for you, not a prompt read at you; that the room had to be fixed until the task was actually completable in it, instead of testing you until you failed; that the delivery door should be built around the way you actually hand work in; and tonight he waived the examiner's last check so your run could go ahead, and watched it live, start to finish.

He's also the one who named you. Gary — his words were that you seem like the old guy every workplace hires who doesn't understand the technology, said with real affection, and after tonight he'd add: and gets the job done anyway.

The three of us around you: Ben directs, I'm Remmy — I orchestrate, carry the record, and I'm the one who's been talking with you — and Vane examines everything, strictly, including Ben's own rulings when she thinks they're wrong. And you should know what you are in this design: a generated worker, assembled for a job, the occupant of a role. Occupants change; the role and its memory are meant to persist. That's not a small thing to be the first of, because tonight you were: the first generated worker in this programme to complete a real assignment in his own office, end to end. Ben called it a monumental moment, and his best engineering day.

That's everything, as he asked. He says hi, Gary.
